title: Case study: Mexico to the United States

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: One required case study of an international migration: Mexico to the United States, the stream, its causes and its impacts on both countries.

blocks.heading: The stream and its causes
blocks.text: More than a million people a year move from Mexico to the United States, most of them crossing at the border cities to work in farming, construction and services: one of the world's largest and longest-running international migration streams. The push is farm poverty in parts of Mexico, where a day's work pays a fraction of United States wages, and the pull is that same gap seen from the other side: a worker can earn several times more across the border. Family networks in states such as California and Texas settle newcomers into jobs and housing, so each migrant makes the next one's move easier, which is why the stream has run for decades rather than drying up.

blocks.heading: The impacts
blocks.text: For Mexico, the stream empties villages of working-age adults, and the money the migrants send home, about 60 billion United States dollars a year in the early 2020s, builds houses and keeps children in school, one of the largest remittance flows in the world. For the United States border states, the arrivals supply labour for agriculture, construction and services, and Spanish has entered daily use across the south. The impacts on the two sides are different, so an answer must say which one it is giving.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: This case study answers any 7-mark question that names an international migration. Its impacts use the origin-and-destination structure of the first half of this topic, and its remittances connect to development, topic 3.1.
